unit.title: Perform advanced welding using gas tungsten arc welding process (GTAW) –Tungsten inert Gas (TIG)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A welder sets DCEP (electrode positive) by mistake for TIG welding stainless steel. What is the most likely result?
options: A deeper, narrower weld than with DCEN
The tungsten overheats and may melt into the weld
No change, because polarity does not matter in TIG
The filler rod will not melt in the pool at all

questions.stem: On an inverter TIG set welding aluminium on AC, the wave is changed to give more electrode-negative time. What happens?
options: More cleaning action and a hotter tungsten
A wider, shallower weld with a dirty look
The arc changes to DC and stops cleaning
Deeper fusion, less cleaning, cooler tungsten

questions.stem: Raising the AC frequency on an inverter TIG set when welding aluminium mainly does what?
options: Narrows and focuses the arc
Widens the arc and the bead
Gives more oxide cleaning
Lowers the welding current

questions.stem: Why do many workshops now use lanthanated or ceriated tungsten in place of thoriated?
options: They can be used without any shielding gas
They are the only kinds that work on DC
They avoid radioactive dust when ground
They never need to be ground to a point

questions.stem: A WPS calls for 150 A on DCEN. The welder has fitted a 1.0 mm tungsten. What is the likely problem?
options: The arc will be too wide to start on the plate
The arc will not start, as the tungsten is too thick
The tungsten overheats and drops into the weld
The gas flow must be doubled for a thin tungsten

questions.stem: Why is the very end of a ground tungsten sometimes given a tiny flat (truncated point)?
options: So the tip does not melt off at higher current
So the tungsten fits a smaller collet body
So that the arc can be struck by scratching
So that it can be used with no gas cup

questions.stem: Why fit a gas lens to the TIG torch for a root run deep in a groove?
options: To make the arc hotter without more current
To filter dust out of the argon from the cylinder
To let the welder use CO2 in place of argon
For smooth gas cover with a longer tungsten stick-out

questions.stem: Which shielding gas helps most when TIG welding 10 mm aluminium, where more heat is needed?
options: Pure carbon dioxide
Argon with helium added
Argon with oxygen added
Pure nitrogen

questions.stem: Why is the inside of a stainless steel pipe purged with argon while the root is TIG welded?
options: To cool the pipe so that it does not distort
To make the weld cap shinier on the outside
To push the filler rod through to the inside
To stop the root oxidising on the inside

questions.stem: A stainless pipe holds 12 litres between the purge dams. The rule used is to pass about 5 times that volume before welding. At 10 L/min, how long should you purge?
options: 1.2 minutes
6 minutes
60 minutes
2 minutes

questions.stem: What is the most reliable way to know a back purge is complete before striking the arc?
options: Count to thirty after turning on the argon
Feel for the gas at the vent with your hand
Measure the oxygen at the vent with a meter
Look for the colour of argon at the vent

questions.stem: Why must a purged pipe have a vent hole?
options: To let gas out so that pressure cannot build up
So that the welder can see the root from inside
So that the filler rod can be fed from inside
So that the pipe cools faster after welding

questions.stem: After welding, the root of a stainless steel joint shows dark blue and grey heat tint. What does this tell you?
options: The purge was poor and the root has oxidised
The weld is perfect and needs no more action
Too little current was used on the root run
The filler rod was the wrong diameter

questions.stem: Which tungsten diameter is a sensible choice for DCEN TIG welding of 3 mm stainless steel at about 90 A?
options: 0.5 mm
4.8 mm
1.6 mm
6.4 mm

questions.stem: Why are low-carbon "L" grade fillers, such as 308L, used on stainless steel?
options: They have more carbon, for a harder weld
Low carbon lowers the risk of weld decay
They melt at a lower temperature than plate
They are lighter and easier to hold

questions.stem: When TIG welding 6061-type aluminium, why is a 4043 or 5356 filler used instead of a filler of the same alloy as the plate?
options: A matching filler costs too much to buy
A matching filler will not melt in the arc
A matching filler only works on a DC arc
A matching filler tends to crack as it cools

questions.stem: Aluminium parts were cleaned yesterday afternoon and left overnight. What should be done before welding this morning?
options: Weld straight away, as cleaning lasts a week
Clean again, as new oxide and dirt will have formed
Heat them red hot to burn off the oxide
Wet them with water to stop more oxide forming

questions.stem: Why may thick aluminium need some preheat before TIG welding?
options: It conducts heat away fast, so fusion is slow to start
It always cracks if it is welded below 30 °C
Preheat removes the need for an AC current
Preheat makes the oxide layer thicker and stronger

questions.stem: What is the main benefit of pulsed TIG on thin stainless steel sheet?
options: It removes the need for a shielding gas
It lets a thoriated tungsten be used on AC
It increases distortion so parts pull together
Less heat, so less distortion

questions.stem: A WPS gives 90–110 A. A welder's test only shows good fusion at 130 A. What is the right action?
options: Weld at 130 A, because the result looks good
Weld at 110 A and travel slower than the WPS allows
Stop and report it so that the procedure is reviewed
Keep 130 A but write 110 A on the weld record

questions.stem: In the 6G pipe position, how is the pipe fixed?
options: Axis horizontal, and the pipe is rolled
Axis vertical, and the weld goes round level
Axis at 45°, and the pipe must not be moved
Axis horizontal, and the pipe is fixed

questions.stem: What does a welder do when "walking the cup" on a TIG pipe joint?
options: Moving the gas cylinder nearer as the weld goes round
Changing the cup size between the root and the cap
Holding the cup clear of the pipe and moving freehand
Rocking the cup on the groove faces to move the torch

questions.stem: When running an open-root TIG pass, what does a small "keyhole" at the front of the pool show?
options: The root is penetrating fully
The tungsten is contaminated
The gas flow is far too high
The filler rod is too thin

questions.stem: Why does a WPS for stainless steel often set a maximum interpass temperature?
options: So that the welder needs no gloves for the next pass
To limit grain growth, distortion and weld decay
So that the shielding gas can be turned down
To keep the tungsten sharp between the passes

questions.stem: How should the interpass temperature be checked?
options: Touch the pipe briefly with a bare hand
Pour water on it and watch for steam
Judge it from the colour of the weld
With a contact thermometer or crayon

questions.stem: Stainless steel sheet distorts more than carbon steel sheet when welded. Why?
options: It has a much softer surface than carbon steel
It is always thinner than carbon steel sheet
It expands more and conducts heat away less
It needs much higher currents than carbon steel

questions.stem: Why are copper chill bars clamped behind thin stainless steel TIG joints?
options: Copper adds alloy to the root of the weld
They draw heat away and support the root
They let the welder leave out the tacks
They help the arc to start more easily

questions.stem: A film radiograph of a TIG weld shows small, very bright white spots. What do they most likely show?
options: Tungsten inclusions
Gas porosity
Lack of side fusion
Undercut on the cap

questions.stem: A TIG root on stainless pipe shows suck-back (the root surface is hollow). Which is a likely cause?
options: Purge pressure too high inside the pipe
Gas flow at the torch slightly too low
Tungsten ground the wrong way round
Using an L-grade filler rod on the root

questions.stem: Aluminium TIG welds keep cracking at the end of each run. Which fix is best?
options: Break the arc quickly and add no filler
Use downslope and add filler to fill the crater
Turn up the current at the end of the run
Switch to DCEN for the last few millimetres

questions.stem: Porosity in aluminium TIG welds is most often caused by what?
options: Too little electrode-negative time on AC
Using argon instead of carbon dioxide
Hydrogen from damp, oil or dirty filler
Using a lanthanated tungsten electrode

questions.stem: Which test is best for finding fine surface cracks in a non-magnetic stainless steel weld?
options: Magnetic particle testing
A hardness test
A tape measure check
Dye penetrant testing

questions.stem: In dye penetrant testing, what is the correct order of steps?
options: Penetrant, clean, developer, remove excess, inspect
Developer, clean, penetrant, inspect, remove excess
Clean, penetrant, remove excess, developer, inspect
Clean, developer, penetrant, remove excess, inspect

questions.stem: Why is radiography (X-ray) often asked for on pipe welds in process lines?
options: It shows flaws inside the weld that cannot be seen
It measures the exact tensile strength of the weld
It cleans the heat tint off the inside of the pipe
It is the only test a welder may do on their own work

questions.stem: An acid paste is used to remove heat tint from stainless steel welds. Which precaution is right?
options: Rinse it into the nearest drain with lots of water
Wear acid-proof gloves and a face shield; follow the SDS
Spread it with bare fingers for better control
Warm it with the TIG torch so it works faster

questions.stem: TIG makes little smoke. Why does TIG welding stainless steel still need good fume control?
options: The fume contains asbestos from the plate
Argon turns into a poisonous gas in the arc
The tungsten gives off carbon monoxide
Its fume holds harmful chromium

questions.stem: A TIG set with high-frequency (HF) starting is used next to a computer-controlled cutting machine. What can happen?
options: The cutting machine will weld itself to its bench
HF can upset nearby electronics and controls
The cutting machine will run faster during welds
Argon will leak out of the machine's air lines

questions.stem: Why do TIG torches for high currents use water cooling?
options: To cool the tungsten so it can be touched
To stop the shielding gas from freezing
To cool the work piece while it is welded
To keep the torch and cable from overheating

questions.stem: During the pre-start check, you find a cracked ceramic cup. What should you do?
options: Wrap it in tape and weld at a lower current
Carry on, as the crack does not affect the gas
Replace it first, as gas cover will be lost
Turn the gas flow up to make up for the crack

questions.stem: Which job is the best fit for TIG rather than MIG?
options: Root run on a thin-wall stainless pipe
Long fillet welds on a heavy steel trailer
Filling a 25 mm thick plate butt quickly
Outdoor repairs on heavy plate in the wind

questions.stem: You are supervising a trainee welding stainless steel. They pick up a wire brush from the mild steel bench. What should you do?
options: Stop them: steel bristles leave iron that rusts
Let them carry on, as any wire brush cleans stainless
Tell them to brush harder to remove more of the oxide
Let them use it, but rinse the brush in water first

questions.stem: Which details must go on the weld record for a stainless pipe joint?
options: Only the date and the welder's first name
The pipe colour and the paint to be used later
Welder, WPS, filler batch, purge and test results
The total weight of argon cylinders in the store

questions.stem: You are planning to TIG weld 20 stainless pipe spools. Which order is the most sensible?
options: Weld all the spools, then check the WPS and materials
Order the filler rod after the welding has started
Test the welds first, then prepare the pipe ends
Check WPS and stock, then prep, fit, weld, test

questions.stem: A TIG run of 600 mm is made at a travel speed of 120 mm/min. How long is the arc time?
options: 0.2 minutes
5 minutes
50 minutes
72 minutes

questions.stem: Why is the tungsten for AC aluminium welding usually larger than one for DC at the same current?
options: AC needs a thicker tungsten to start the HF spark
A larger tungsten gives more oxide cleaning action
The electrode-positive half of AC heats the tungsten
Aluminium needs a heavier tungsten to push the pool

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Describe how you would prepare, purge and weld the root of a butt joint in 50 mm stainless steel tube with TIG, so that the inside of the root is sound and free of heavy oxide.
essays.modelAnswer: I would check the tube grade and the WPS, then cut the ends square, bevel or square-edge them as the WPS says and remove all burrs. I would clean the inside and outside with a solvent and a stainless brush kept only for stainless. I would fit purge dams on each side of the joint, tape the joint gap and put a small vent at the far side. I would purge with argon at the flow in the WPS and pass several times the inside volume, then check the oxygen at the vent with a meter if one is available. I would remove the tape a little at a time as I tack and weld, keeping the purge running. I would weld the root with a sharp tungsten, a gas lens and the correct current, adding filler steadily so that the root is fully fused and slightly convex. I would keep the purge on for the hot pass. Afterwards I would check the inside for colour: silver to light straw is good; dark blue or grey means the purge failed.
markingPoints: Checks grade and WPS; prepares, deburrs and cleans with a stainless-only brush
Fits purge dams and a vent; tapes the gap
Purges enough volume and checks oxygen before welding
Welds root with correct settings, keeps purge on for the next pass
Inspects root colour and knows what dark heat tint means

essays.stem: Explain why aluminium is TIG welded on AC, and describe how the balance and frequency settings change the weld.
essays.modelAnswer: Aluminium is covered in a tough oxide layer that melts at a much higher temperature than the aluminium under it. On AC the current changes direction many times a second. In the electrode-positive part, the arc breaks up the oxide on the plate: this is the cleaning action. In the electrode-negative part, most of the heat goes into the plate, giving penetration, and the tungsten stays cooler. The balance control sets how much time is spent in each part. More electrode-negative time gives deeper fusion, a narrower bead and a cooler tungsten, but less cleaning. More electrode-positive time gives more cleaning, a wider frosted band and a hotter tungsten, which may then ball or spit. The frequency control sets how many times a second the current changes. A higher frequency gives a narrower, more focused arc that is easier to direct into a corner. A lower frequency gives a wider, softer arc. The settings are chosen to suit the job and the WPS.
markingPoints: Oxide layer melts far hotter than aluminium and must be broken up
Electrode-positive part cleans; electrode-negative part gives heat into the work
Balance: more EN = more fusion, less cleaning, cooler tungsten
More EP = more cleaning, hotter tungsten
Frequency: higher narrows and focuses the arc; lower widens it

essays.stem: Compare the common types of tungsten electrode, say how you would choose one for a job, and explain the safe way to grind them.
essays.modelAnswer: Pure tungsten was traditionally used for AC on transformer sets, where its end forms a ball, but it carries less current. Thoriated tungsten starts well and carries high current on DC, but it contains a little radioactive thorium, so the grinding dust must not be breathed. Ceriated tungsten starts well at low current and works on AC and DC. Lanthanated tungsten works well on AC and DC and is a common all-round choice in place of thoriated. Zirconiated tungsten resists contamination on AC. To choose, I would follow the WPS, then think about the current type, the current level and the metal. The diameter must suit the current. I would grind on a wheel kept only for tungsten, with the grinding marks running along the length towards the point, and a taper of about two to three times the diameter. I would wear safety glasses, use local extraction or a dust-collecting grinder, and dispose of the dust as the Centre's rules say.
markingPoints: Describes at least three types and their main uses
Thoriated is radioactive: control grinding dust
Chooses by WPS, AC or DC, current level and metal; diameter suits current
Grinds lengthwise on a dedicated wheel to a suitable taper
Glasses, extraction or dust collection, safe disposal

essays.stem: Explain why heat control matters when TIG welding thin stainless steel, and describe the methods you would use to limit distortion and protect corrosion resistance.
essays.modelAnswer: Stainless steel expands more than carbon steel and conducts heat away more slowly, so heat stays in one place and the sheet distorts more. If it is kept hot for too long, chromium joins with carbon next to the weld, and that area can rust later (weld decay). Heavy heat also gives dark heat tint, which lowers corrosion resistance. To control this I would use a low-carbon L-grade filler and the lowest current that gives full fusion. I would use pulsed TIG if available. I would clamp the work to copper chill bars, which draw heat away and support the root. I would tack closely and evenly, weld short runs in a balanced or skip order, and let the work cool to the WPS interpass temperature, checking it with a contact thermometer. I would keep good gas cover on the back as well as the front. After welding I would remove heat tint by brushing with a stainless brush or by pickling.
markingPoints: Higher expansion and lower conductivity cause more distortion
Weld decay and heat tint reduce corrosion resistance
Low current, pulse, L-grade filler
Chill bars, close tacks, balanced or skip sequence, interpass control
Back shielding and removal of heat tint after welding

essays.stem: Explain what heat tint on stainless steel welds is, why it must be removed on many jobs, and how to remove it safely.
essays.modelAnswer: Heat tint is the coloured oxide that forms on stainless steel next to and on the weld when it is hot and meets air. The colours run from light straw through gold, purple and blue to grey. The darker the colour, the thicker the oxide and the more chromium has been taken from the surface, so the steel there can rust or stain. On food, water and chemical work the specification usually says it must be removed. It can be removed by brushing with a stainless steel brush used only for stainless, by fine grinding or polishing, or by pickling with an acid paste or gel. Pickling paste is strong acid, so I would read the SDS, wear acid-proof gloves, a face shield, long sleeves and an apron, and work with good ventilation. I would leave it on only for the time the maker says, rinse it off as the SDS says, and collect the waste for proper disposal, never pouring it down a drain. Prevention is better: good gas cover and back purging.
markingPoints: Defines heat tint as oxide colours from straw to grey
Darker colour = less chromium at the surface = rust risk
Removal by stainless brush, polishing or pickling
Pickling safety: SDS, gloves, face shield, ventilation, timed contact
Proper waste disposal; prevention by good shielding and purging

essays.stem: A batch of aluminium brackets TIG welded by your team shows porosity and crater cracks. Explain how you would investigate, correct the problem and record what was done.
essays.modelAnswer: I would stop welding that batch and set aside the faulty brackets. For porosity, I would look for sources of hydrogen and air. I would check how the aluminium and filler were cleaned and stored, whether the filler rod was dirty or damp, whether gloves were oily, and whether parts were cleaned and then left too long. I would check the argon flow, the hose and fittings for leaks, the cup size and any draughts. For crater cracks, I would watch how each welder ends the run: whether they use downslope and add filler to fill the crater, and whether the filler grade suits the alloy. I would correct the faults, clean and store materials properly, set the crater-fill or downslope, and coach the welders. I would have them weld test pieces and check them, then repair the brackets to an approved method. I would record what was found, the cause, the action taken and the results, and report to my supervisor.
markingPoints: Stops the batch and keeps the faulty parts
Porosity: checks cleaning, filler condition, gloves, gas flow, leaks, draughts
Crater cracks: checks crater filling, downslope and filler grade
Corrects, coaches, tests and repairs to an approved method
Records cause, action and results; reports to the supervisor

essays.stem: Describe how a TIG-welded stainless steel pipe joint would be inspected and tested, and what records would be kept.
essays.modelAnswer: Inspection starts before welding: checking the material grade, the WPS, the fit-up, the root gap, the alignment (hi-lo) and the cleanliness. During welding, the purge, the current and the interpass temperature are checked. After welding, the outside is inspected visually for the cap size and shape, undercut, porosity, cracks and heat tint. The inside of the root is checked with a mirror, a torch or a borescope for full penetration, suck-back and the colour of the root. Dye penetrant testing can be used to find fine surface cracks, because stainless steel of this kind is not magnetic. Radiography may be asked for to find flaws inside the weld such as porosity, inclusions or lack of fusion. A pressure test may be done on the finished spool. The records include the joint number, welder, WPS, filler batch, purge details, inspection and test results, repairs and retests, signed and dated.
markingPoints: Checks before welding: material, WPS, fit-up and cleanliness
Checks during welding: purge, current, interpass
Visual inspection outside and inside the root
Dye penetrant and radiography, with what each finds
Records: joint, welder, WPS, filler, purge, results, repairs; signed and dated

essays.stem: Describe the health and safety hazards of TIG welding stainless steel and aluminium at the Centre, and the controls for each.
essays.modelAnswer: The arc gives strong ultraviolet light that burns eyes and skin, so I would wear a helmet with the correct shade, cover all skin and use screens to protect others. With aluminium, the UV also makes ozone, which irritates the lungs, so good ventilation or extraction is needed. Stainless steel fume contains chromium and nickel compounds that can harm health, so local extraction close to the arc is used. Grinding thoriated tungsten makes radioactive dust, so a dedicated grinder with dust collection, or a non-thoriated type, is used. High-frequency starting can affect pacemakers and electronics, so people with medical implants should take advice and stay clear. Electric shock is controlled by checking cables and keeping PPE dry. Argon can push out oxygen in a closed space, so cylinders are kept upright and secured, leaks checked, and confined spaces need a permit and gas testing. Pickling paste is strong acid and needs gloves, a face shield and the SDS. I would always follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: UV: correct shade, covered skin, screens; ozone with aluminium needs ventilation
Chromium and nickel fume from stainless: local extraction
Thoriated dust and HF effects on implants and electronics
Electric shock and gas cylinder or oxygen displacement controls
Pickling acid PPE and SDS; maker's instructions and Centre rules

essays.stem: Explain how you would coach and check a less experienced welder who is TIG welding stainless steel pipe to a WPS for the first time.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would go through the WPS with them and make sure they understand the current range, tungsten, filler, gas flow, purge and interpass limits. I would check that their qualification covers the job, or arrange for them to practise and be tested first. I would show them how to set up the machine and the purge, and let them do it while I watch. I would have them weld a practice joint on offcuts of the same pipe, watching their torch angle, arc length, filler adding and how they keep the tungsten clean. I would cut or inspect the practice joint with them and explain what was good and what to improve. On the real job I would check their fit-up and purge before they weld, and check the root before the next pass. I would give feedback calmly and in private where needed. I would record their work and the inspection results, and tell my supervisor how they are progressing.
markingPoints: Explains the WPS ranges and checks qualification
Demonstrates set-up, then watches them do it
Practice joint with observation and feedback
Checks fit-up, purge and root at hold points on the real job
Constructive feedback, records and reports progress

essays.stem: Explain what you would check in a TIG WPS before starting a job, and what you should do if one of its conditions cannot be met at the Centre.
essays.modelAnswer: I would check that the WPS matches the job: the parent material grade and thickness or pipe size, the joint type and preparation, and the welding positions. I would check the process, the current type and polarity, the current and voltage ranges and the travel speed or heat input. I would check the tungsten type and size, the filler grade and size, the shielding gas and flow, and any back purge. I would check the preheat and the maximum interpass temperature, any heat treatment, and the inspection and testing needed. I would also check that the welders are qualified to it. If a condition cannot be met, for example the right filler grade is not in stock or the purge equipment is not available, I must not change it myself or carry on and hope. I would stop, tell my supervisor, and wait for an approved answer: the right materials, or a different WPS that has been qualified. I would record what happened.
markingPoints: Material, thickness, joint and positions match the job
Process, polarity, current ranges, travel speed or heat input
Tungsten, filler, gas, purge, preheat and interpass, tests
Checks welders are qualified to it
If a condition cannot be met: stop, report, wait for an approved change; record

practical1.title: TIG weld stainless steel tube butt joints with an argon back purge, then inspect and record them
practical1.brief: As a team, read the WPS the assessor gives you for TIG welding 304 or 316 stainless steel tube (about 50 mm outside diameter, 2–3 mm wall) and write a short plan: the preparation, the purge set-up and purge time (show the working), the settings, the inspection points and who does what. Prepare the tube ends, clean them with stainless-only brushes and solvent, and set up the purge dams, tape and vent. Each member welds one butt joint in the position the assessor sets (2G or 5G), with the purge running, while the assessor watches. Members take turns to check another member's fit-up and purge before welding. When each joint has cooled, cut it in half lengthways (or use a mirror or borescope) so that the inside of the root can be seen, and record the root colour, penetration and any faults on the weld record. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the joints, the records and the clean-up are finished.
materials: Stainless steel tube, about 50 mm OD, 2–3 mm wall, cut into short lengths (2 per member)
WPS from the assessor, plan sheet and weld record sheets
TIG set with DC output, gas lens, 1.6 mm or 2.4 mm tungsten, matching L-grade filler rod
Argon cylinders and flowmeters for torch and purge; purge dams or bungs, tape
Oxygen meter for the purge, if the Centre has one
Stainless-only wire brushes, solvent and clean cloths
Bandsaw or cut-off saw to section the joints, mirror or borescope
photos: The plan with the purge time worked out
Tube ends prepared and cleaned, with the stainless-only brushes
The purge set-up: dams, tape and vent in place
A member welding a joint in full PPE
All finished joints labelled with each member's name
Sectioned joints showing the inside of each root
checklist: Helped plan the job and worked out the purge time correctly
Prepared and cleaned the tube ends without contaminating them
Set up a working purge and checked it before striking the arc
Set the machine within the WPS ranges
Made a root with full penetration and light-coloured root oxide
Made a cap of even width with no undercut, porosity or tungsten contamination
Checked a team member's fit-up and recorded results accurately
Wore the right PPE throughout and left the area safe and tidy
safety: Weld behind screens; cover all skin against UV; use the correct filter shade
Use local fume extraction: stainless fume contains chromium compounds
Chain argon cylinders upright and check fittings for leaks; argon can push out oxygen
Use solvent away from the arc, with ventilation, and store it closed
Wear safety glasses and keep hands clear when sawing the joints
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Fabricate an aluminium bracket assembly on AC TIG and check it with dye penetrant
practical2.brief: As a team, make an aluminium bracket assembly to the drawing the assessor gives you: a base plate about 200 mm × 150 mm with two upright gussets and a top plate, in 4–6 mm aluminium, using fillet and corner joints. First, write a short plan: the cutting list, the filler grade, the AC settings (current, balance and frequency, from the WPS), the tack and weld sequence, and who does what. Clean the parts by degreasing and then brushing with a stainless brush kept for aluminium. Each member tacks or welds at least two joints while the assessor watches. Check the assembly for size and squareness against the drawing. Then carry out a dye penetrant test on at least two welds, as the maker's instructions say, and record the results with a sketch on an inspection sheet. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the assembly, the inspection sheet and the clean-up are finished.
materials: Aluminium plate, 4–6 mm, cut to the drawing
Drawing and WPS from the assessor, plan sheet and inspection sheet
